query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted aging treatment that promotes a uniform, nanoscale Al-rich L12 precipitate distribution within the FCC lamellae will enhance the alloy’s high-temperature stability, creep resistance, and corrosion performance without compromising its strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy produced by conventional casting or laser cladding that features a fine lamellar microstructure consisting of FCC (with some L12) and BCC/B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Perform an optimized step-aging heat treatment (e.g., holding at about 900 °C for a controlled duration under an inert atmosphere followed by controlled cooling) to intentionally promote fine, uniformly distributed Al-rich L12 precipitates in the FCC phase.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be applied after initial processing (casting/laser cladding) while avoiding excessive grain growth; it is to be conducted under inert conditions to prevent unwanted oxidation and must be tuned such that the precipitate size remains in the nanoscale regime.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined dispersion of nanoscale Al-rich L12 precipitates within the ductile FCC lamellae that acts to pin dislocations and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The uniformly dispersed, nanoscale L12 precipitates will hinder dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, thereby enhancing resistance to deformation under long-term mechanical loading and high-temperature fluctuations, while also contributing to a more stable and protective oxide scale that improves corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the conventionally processed alloy, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit a superior balance of strength and ductility, reduced room-temperature creep rates, and improved resistance against corrosion (evidenced by lower oxide spallation levels) under extreme operating conditions.
generation.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, as processed by conventional techniques, whose microstructure is not optimized for nanoscale precipitate strengthening and consequently does not meet certain industrial performance criteria.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only if the aging treatment parameters (temperature and time) are finely controlled; excessive aging may lead to precipitate coarsening or grain growth that could negate the benefits. The improvement may be limited if the processing conditions cannot maintain the nanoscale morphology of the precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aging time and temperature for maximized precipitate refinement without inducing detrimental grain coarsening remain to be determined. Additionally, the long-term stability of these precipitates under cyclic temperature conditions and mechanical loading requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples using the same conventional processing method. Subject one set to the proposed optimized step-aging heat treatment while keeping the second set as a control. Then, perform a battery of tests including long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep tests, and high-temperature corrosion experiments. Characterize the microstructure using electron microscopy (e.g., TEM, SEM) to verify the distribution and size of the precipitates.
measurements: Tensile strength and ductility measurements to assess the strength–ductility balance
Creep rate determination at room temperature under constant load
Corrosion tests, including quantification of oxide scale adhesion and spallation area after exposure to corrosive environments
Microstructural analysis (precipitate size distribution, grain boundary characteristics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in creep resistance, corrosion performance, and/or mechanical properties (strength and ductility) compared to the control group, or if the treatment leads to detrimental microstructural changes (e.g., significant precipitate coarsening), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, the Y and Hf co-doping did not change the microstructure morphology and phase structure of the coatings but did improve the thermal stability and resistance of the hot corrosion oxide scale spallation, providing a certain amount of data and theoretical support for the application of EHEA coat

## Abstract
AbstractPhase-specific damage tolerance was investigated for the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high entropy alloy with a lamellar microstructure of L12 and B2 phases. A microcantilever bending technique was utilized with notches milled in each of the two phases as well as at the phase boundary. The L12 phase exhibited superior bending strength, strain hardening, and plastic deformation, while the B2 phase showed limited damage tolerance during bending due to micro-crack formation. The dimensionalized stiffness (DS) of the L12 phase cantilevers were relatively constant, indicating strain hardening followed by increase in stiffness at the later stages and, therefore, indicating plastic failure. In contrast, the B2 phase cantilevers showed a continuous drop in stiffness, indicating crack propagation. ## Abstract
Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
